title: Child with meningitis, parent refuses care: contact child protective services
vignette: A 3-year-old boy is brought to the emergency department due to a fever and stiff neck. The child is hospitalized with a diagnosis of bacterial meningitis and begins treatment with intravenous antibiotics. On day 2 of hospitalization, the mother requests to take the child home and explains that she intends to treat him with homeopathic remedies. She has 4 other children at home who have "never needed vaccinations or medications" and are "strong and healthy." The physician explains the risks of meningitis, including brain damage and death. After a long discussion, the mother says that she understands the risks but believes that homeopathic remedies will be adequate for treatment and remains unconvinced of the need for hospitalization. Which of the following is the most appropriate course of action?

clues.note: Untreated bacterial meningitis is a medical emergency that can rapidly cause brain damage and death - so the stakes are high enough to override parental refusal to protect the child.

clues.text: intends to treat him with homeopathic remedies
clues.note: The parent wants to substitute an ineffective therapy for proven, life-saving antibiotics in a young child - a refusal that endangers the child, not merely the parent.

clues.text: understands the risks but believes that homeopathic remedies will be adequate
clues.note: The mother demonstrates understanding and reasoning, so she is not incompetent - decision-making capacity is intact. The issue is that her choice would harm the child, not that she lacks capacity.

clues.text: remains unconvinced of the need for hospitalization
clues.note: Collaboration and education have failed. When a parent cannot be persuaded and the child faces serious harm, the physician must protect the child - continue treatment and involve child protective services.

whatMatters: A parent may refuse treatment for herself but not withhold life-saving care from a child. Bacterial meningitis is lethal untreated; when education/collaboration fail, the physician must act in the child's best interest - continue IV antibiotics and involve CHILD PROTECTIVE SERVICES. Answer C. Parental autonomy is overridden to prevent serious harm to a minor.
strategy: Apply the pediatric-refusal rule: the child's best interest overrides parental autonomy when refusal risks serious harm/death. Meningitis is life-threatening, so you cannot discharge (D/E) or offer unproven home substitutes (B). Capacity isn't the issue - she understands and reasons (so A is a distractor). After failed persuasion: keep treating and contact CPS = C.

options.text: Arrange for a psychiatric evaluation to assess the mother's decision-making capacity
Arrange for a visiting nurse to administer intravenous antibiotics at home
Contact child protective services while continuing intravenous antibiotics
Discharge against medical advice with instructions to return if the child's condition deteriorates
Discharge the patient on oral antibiotics with daily in-home check ups

eliminations.label: Psychiatric evaluation of capacity - not the issue
eliminations.detail: WHAT IT IS: a capacity assessment gauges whether a decision-maker understands and reasons about a choice. ❌ WHY IT FAILS: the mother clearly understands the risks and gives a coherent (if misguided) rationale - her capacity isn't in question. ✅ Correct if: the parent were altered/incompetent or unable to understand.

eliminations.label: Home IV antibiotics via visiting nurse - unsafe/not agreed
eliminations.detail: WHAT IT IS: home IV therapy for a stable patient needing convenient access. ❌ WHY IT FAILS: the mother rejects antibiotics altogether in favor of homeopathy, and a child with meningitis needs hospital-level monitoring for complications. ✅ Correct if: a stable patient who accepts IV antibiotics but needs home access.

eliminations.label: Discharge against medical advice - your pick
eliminations.detail: WHAT IT IS: AMA discharge lets a competent patient leave against recommendations. ❌ WHY IT FAILS: a parent cannot sign a child out against advice when doing so risks death - AMA applies to a competent patient refusing their OWN care, not a guardian endangering a child. ✅ Correct if: an adult with capacity were refusing treatment for himself.

eliminations.label: Discharge on oral antibiotics + home checks - inadequate
eliminations.detail: WHAT IT IS: oral antibiotics with outpatient follow-up. ❌ WHY IT FAILS: oral agents don't reliably treat bacterial meningitis (inadequate CSF penetration), and the mother hasn't agreed to give them; unsafe. ✅ Correct if: a mild infection treatable with orals and reliable follow-up.

reasoning: Untreated bacterial meningitis can cause brain damage and death - a serious threat to the child
A parent cannot refuse life-saving care for a child (best-interest standard overrides autonomy)
Education and collaboration have already failed
-> continue IV antibiotics and involve child protective services; answer C
mechanism: Physicians have an ethical and legal duty to act in a child's best interest. Parental authority to make medical decisions can be overridden when a refusal exposes the child to serious harm or death, as with untreated bacterial meningitis. The preferred first step is collaboration - educating and negotiating with the parent (and, if helpful, involving an ethics committee) - but when that fails, the physician should continue necessary treatment and involve a state child protective agency (seeking a court order if needed). Decision-making capacity is not the issue here (the mother understands the risks and articulates a rationale), so psychiatric evaluation is unnecessary; and discharge in any form (against medical advice, oral antibiotics, or home IV) would place the child at unacceptable risk. Note the contrast with a competent ADULT, who may refuse treatment for himself and leave against medical advice.

difficulty.label: 📚 Pure knowledge gap
difficulty.message: First Aid Ethics > parental refusal and the best-interest standard; when to involve CPS/court; capacity criteria; emancipated/mature minor exceptions; emergency exception.

difficulty.label: 🧭 Understanding the question
difficulty.message: The scenario is a FAILED collaboration with a capable parent whose choice endangers the child - so protect the child, not reassess capacity.

difficulty.label: 🔤 Vocabulary
difficulty.message: Unsure on 'against medical advice,' decision-making capacity, best-interest standard, or child protective services? Tell me which.

difficulty.label: 🧲 Pulled by a distractor
difficulty.message: Your pick (AMA discharge) applies to competent ADULTS refusing their OWN care. Option A is wrong because capacity is intact. B and E are unsafe substitutes for hospital IV therapy.

difficulty.label: ✍️ Something else
difficulty.message: Bank: you can refuse care for yourself, not life-saving care for your child; after failed persuasion in a lethal illness, continue treatment + contact CPS.
